Research date: October 18, 2026. Baseline: Fieldguide 0.31.15 / matching engine 3.3.0.

What I recommend

Keep Fieldguide a friendly guide: picture a life, understand interests, explore a few paths, and leave with one useful plan. Its strongest feature is the connection between career interests, realistic training routes, Austin living costs, and saved next steps. The next improvement should be better evidence and fewer required follow-ups, rather than a larger survey or a school-management platform.

The official interest assessment gives us a credible foundation. Our added matching rules are transparent and extensively checked in software, but have not been validated with real students. Our career coverage is much smaller than the major databases. Most displayed salary milestones are financial scenarios, rather than observed earnings after exactly 5, 10, or 20 years. These are the most consequential areas to improve.

This report proposes priorities. It does not change the student questionnaire, matching rules, money estimates, or navigation.

Scope and evidence

Three parallel research agents reviewed assessment services, school/college platforms, and consumer/financial guidance. The lead review audited Fieldguide's source, question bank, career catalog, finance functions, and retained verification records, and added major-selection and performance-assessment comparators. Together these cover 27 services, plus authoritative financial references. This is a broad relevant review, not a claim to cover every service worldwide or rank products by market share.

Competitor evidence comes from official documentation, technical reports, sample reports, policies, and published research. Most paid or school-authenticated experiences were not walked through. Princeton Review's anonymous opening screen was observed; its full results were not. Fieldguide has a developer-conducted mobile browser walkthrough, not a comparative study with teenagers. Vendor time estimates are identified as estimates. An undocumented feature or coefficient means unverified in this review, not absent.

Detailed research accompanies this report:

  • Assessment services: O*NET, CareerOneStop, YouScience, Morrisby, Kuder, Strong, Highlands
  • School and college platforms, plus Appily, Niche, CollegeVine
  • Consumer guidance, financial sources, access and pricing
  • Additional comparators: MyMajors, Johnson O'Connor, ASVAB
  • Financial methods: source definitions and a concrete pay discrepancy
  • Student outcomes: independent studies versus marketing measures

The annexes preserve individual researchers' suggestions; this synthesis resolves conflicts. In particular, we should not replace the official instrument with an unvalidated handful of questions, force three suggestions, restore an unwanted answer choice, or make the required lifestyle step optional merely because a comparator does so.

What our matching engine really does

The six RIASEC scores describe Realistic, Investigative, Artistic, Social, Enterprising and Conventional interests. Fieldguide totals the official responses into six 0–40 scores, then compares the complete six-dimensional pattern with occupation interest vectors using Pearson correlation. This compares the shape of the profile; it is not a skill score or a chance of success. Full-profile correlation is consistent with O*NET's documented linkage approach. O*NET career-return methodology, October 2025

Our additional decisions are custom: a broad family's score uses its three strongest distinct occupation correlations; repeated daily-work evidence supports pathway recommendations; profession questions distinguish roles and surface working-condition or education conflicts. Strong repeated task interest can retain a sensible career even where the general RIASEC match is weak. Experience answers describe familiarity and next steps rather than excluding beginners. The app can show fewer than three supported pathways.

This architecture is reasonable, but several choices need calibration:

  • A broad family with more varied occupations has more opportunities to produce high correlations. Changes to catalog composition can change family results even if a student gives identical answers.
  • Several similar custom questions can exaggerate support if they are treated as independent evidence. Count distinct domains as well as question IDs.
  • Numeric thresholds borrowed from occupation matching do not automatically validate averages of family scores or our custom rules.
  • Role-specific gates can accidentally hide a sensible profession. Writing and food service already illustrate why task evidence deserves a route through weak broad-profile matching.
  • Family-level labels are often too broad to be decisive: liking helping people does not distinguish physician, nurse, therapist and teacher. Relevant daily work and training differences should refine these choices.
  • A lifestyle gap should alter the financial explanation, not silently rewrite the interest profile. Required lifestyle-first ordering may prime pay preferences; test this order effect without changing the user's chosen flow by assumption.

Accuracy is several different questions

Evidence layerWhat it can establishFieldguide's position
Instrument reliability/validityWhether a particular form measures its intended construct consistently for an intended populationPublished O*NET evidence supports the core instrument; its manual recommends approximately age 14+, eighth-grade reading and familiarity with work activities. Version and intended use still matter.
Implementation correctnessScores, navigation, data definitions and calculations work as specifiedReference scoring, source audits and software/browser checks provide evidence.
Recommendation qualitySuggested paths are sensible, relevant, sufficiently varied, and not prematurely restrictiveAuthored student scenarios and sensitivity checks help find defects; independent student/counselor evaluation is missing.
Real-world usefulnessStudents understand results, try relevant activities and make better-informed decisionsNot yet measured in a student pilot.
Prediction calibrationA stated probability matches an observed outcome frequencyWe do not have such evidence and should not label match strength as a probability.

The current record contains 54 authored scenarios with 38 distinct score patterns, 5,820 one-step answer perturbations, and 12 later developer-authored narratives. These are useful engineering checks, not thousands of independent students. The recent phone change has 109 targeted regression checks; older release-wide records have different scopes. Real-student pilot participants: zero. Sensitivity record, additional narratives

Competitors do not provide one comparable “accuracy” number either. Strong publishes detailed scale and occupation-similarity methods; Kuder publishes a student-focused technical brief; Unifrog discloses review procedures; PathwayU discusses research and an earlier portal intervention. These differ in population, version and outcome. They cannot be converted into a defensible accuracy leaderboard. Strong methods, Kuder evidence, Unifrog review process, PathwayU science

What independent outcome studies add

MDRC's August 2026 school study of Xello/YouScience found no significant positive effect on its primary CTE-concentration outcome, with some negative secondary comparisons. It used matching after planned randomization was disrupted, pooled implementations, and had important usage/control limitations. It neither proves the current products ineffective nor validates individual matches. For us, it argues for testing understanding and real next actions, beyond producing a report. MDRC final study

Independent Naviance research also shows that information design can change choices in unintended ways. A 2023 PNAS study associated historical scattergram access with more application undermatching among high-achieving applicants. It was observational, concerns college applications rather than career fit, and is not a current-platform trial. Fieldguide should test whether a small suggestion list discourages viable alternatives. Original PNAS paper

The deeper outcome annex also checks vendor metrics. MajorClarity's “189%” headline concerns odds of plan selection in an observational study; Xello's 78% plan-impact figure is educators' opinion, not a measured student completion rate. Neither is a personalized-match accuracy rate. Preserve original denominators and separate activity, satisfaction, behavior and causal benefit. Outcome evidence and original sources

A large interest-fit study found profile correlations explained about 4% of career-choice-satisfaction variance in its sample. That is not “4% accuracy,” a result about our app, or evidence that interests are useless. It illustrates why one interest fit score should not decide a student's future. Primary study, published online October 2024

Length: our most immediate usability risk

Source-derived authored examples require 108 question/choice screens for creative work, 115 for medicine and 122 for trades, including nine lifestyle choices and the selected profession branch, excluding transition screens. This is not an observed average across students. The adaptive profile selects from a bank of 60 official items, 36 custom activity items, 12 experience questions, one priorities screen and four context questions. One family branch adds eight profession questions; health adds eleven.

The official 60-item component alone is estimated at 5–20 minutes in the manual. We therefore cannot credibly promise that the full current journey takes ten minutes. Short prompts and auto-advance reduce interaction cost; they do not remove the cognitive effort of 100-plus decisions.

Recommended sequence, retaining lifestyle first:

  1. Keep the nine friendly lifestyle choices and end tally.
  2. Keep the existing official interest assessment intact while measuring actual completion.
  3. Keep a short, balanced daily-work pass across broad families; offer initial supported pathways without requiring every experience/context detail.
  4. Ask deeper questions only in the chosen field, including one real tradeoff that distinguishes plausible professions.
  5. Put experience questions and nonessential refinement after the first useful result where they improve next steps. Preserve optional access to every question in Developer review.
  6. End with one saved plan and a short next action. Allow further exploration without restarting or repeating introductions.

This is a proposed sequencing change, not implemented in this research task. Do not remove the broad task pass so aggressively that students with strong task interests but weak general correlations disappear from the results.

Should we use the official 30-item form?

It is worth evaluating as a separate, versioned option. It is not the same as selecting our favorite 30 of the existing 60. The published Mini-IP validation comparison reports lower internal consistency than the 60-item form: .74–.81 versus .85–.90 in that adult comparison sample. That does not quantify teen decision accuracy, but does document a precision/burden tradeoff. Keep the 60-item release until we deliberately compare official forms and outcomes. Preserve official wording, labels, scoring, attribution and applicable license requirements. Mini-IP development report, tool license

Set time goals only as hypotheses to test: a useful first result in roughly 15 minutes and a personal plan in roughly 20–25 minutes, with easy pause/resume. The retained 60-item version may exceed them. Measure active time, total elapsed time, breaks and drop-off separately before advertising a time promise.

Financial data: where our integration helps and where precision misleads

Across the 117 full careers, the current progression function returns 113 modeled local-wage scenarios and four published-employer-schedule examples. Geography is Austin-related for 116; one uses Dallas–Fort Worth. Most modeled progressions interpolate from an entry proxy toward a Texas Workforce Commission experienced-worker anchor. Five-, ten- and twenty-year milestones use assumed fractions of that gap. Those fractions were not fitted to longitudinal career histories. TWC defines entry as the mean of the lowest-paid third and experienced as the mean of the upper-paid two-thirds; neither is a tenure band. TWC definitions

Concrete refresh item: the runtime still uses $66,019 for Austin Fire post-academy entry; the same official page retrieved October 18 states $67,999. It does not date that change, so this is a saved-versus-current-source discrepancy, not proof the earlier review was wrong. Refresh the named employer example and reconcile later-stage assumptions; do not replace the separate TWC occupation anchor with the employer amount. No salary code was changed in this research task. Current city source

Keep the user's useful entry / 5 / 10 / 20 display, but describe it plainly as estimated starting pay and possible pay with experience. A compact “Pay estimate” marker can link to the method. Where an actual schedule applies, state the employer and year. Avoid suggesting guaranteed raises, exact milestones or total compensation. For physician routes, distinguish paid residency from later qualified practice; for self-employment, distinguish revenue from personal income. Retained salary design, current finance review

TopicBest benchmarkWhat the student should see
WagesBLS OEWS / TWC occupation data; employer schedules where relevantRounded estimate, place/year, and plain annual-hours assumptions. Wage percentiles are not experience years; OEWS excludes self-employed workers and nonwage benefits. BLS definitions
Austin baselineMIT Living Wage, same household and price yearA basic-needs comparison, not a comfortable lifestyle promise. Travis County's February 2026 model is $49,279 gross for one adult/no children. Its baseline excludes vacations, dining out and savings. Our chosen-lifestyle total must reconcile definitions before comparison. County baseline, methodology
Lifestyle fitIndependently recomputed budget and take-home pay“Starting pay is below your budget,” “It covers your budget with little left,” or “It covers your budget with room to save,” based on assumptions. Show the gap or margin; do not call this an estimated probability of affording life.
Tuition and aidNamed program cost/attendance budget, institutional net-price calculator, Federal Student AidCost before aid; estimated grants/scholarships; what remains; loans separately. A general career-route example is not a personalized offer. UT calculator, aid offers
Program outcomesCollege Scorecard/IPEDS, with cohort definitionsEducation-route comparisons behind More info. Earnings by college/program are not a personal wage promise or proof that a degree caused the difference. Scorecard documentation

Our income-goal range currently includes a planning buffer; it is not a statistical confidence interval. Rent/own deposits and down payments need to remain separate from recurring bills. Aid and loans must not be subtracted twice. The realistic conclusion may change with part-time hours, insurance, retirement saving, loan payments or a different rent. Use those sensitivities to calibrate the result, while keeping the student screen brief.

College benefits should be specific: “A nursing degree can open the RN route” is useful; a universal claim that any degree raises earnings in every trade is not. Explain advancement, licensing, transfer options or business skills when supported, alongside time and cost. Keep strong college opportunities visible without weakening truthful non-college routes.

MIT's county page requests no scraping and provides licensing information. This review uses it as a linked benchmark, not permission to import its dataset. Texas Reality Check provides useful interaction ideas, but its housing, debt and family assumptions should not be adopted unquestioningly. MIT county source, Texas assumptions

Results and presentation: add usefulness without adding clutter

Keep a small first layer. Each pathway/career card needs a recognizable icon, a clear name, an everyday description, two short reasons, and a separate lifestyle verdict. A low-confidence or unfamiliar answer should invite an activity, not produce a “not capable” label. Display fewer pathways when fewer are supported.

The detailed career page should answer: What would I do? What training would I need? What would it cost? What might I earn? Does that cover my chosen life? What can I try next? Put assumptions, distributions, conflicting preferences, sources and alternative routes behind More info. Related uncommon jobs can sit within the same field, clearly distinguished from the fully researched anchor career.

The final plan should focus on the student's current direction, education/training route, money fit and three next steps. Keep previous interests, notes and completed work. Allow a new career choice to update requirements and finances without erasing earlier exploration. Retain the standalone career library as information collection, rather than adding more competing entry points into the guided route.

Do not copy personality-type identities, enormous PDF-style reports, admissions odds, recruitment feeds, counselor dashboards or every available psychometric module. Those add scope and interpretation risks without solving our current student task. Optional task videos and small career experiments are more useful than a second mandatory personality inventory.

Research and calibration plan

These are proposed studies and checks, not completed validation. Intended-use validity and fairness require evidence about the actual population, version and decision being supported. A famous framework or a high assertion count is insufficient. AERA/APA/NCME Testing Standards

PriorityWorkUseful completion evidence
1. Measure burden and comprehensionStart with 5–8 student cognitive interviews on phones. Include mixed interests, low exposure/confidence, trades and professional routes. Then a broader usability pilot, initially 20–30 students.Measured time to first useful result/plan, pauses/drop-off by section, direct answer-editing success, and ability to explain the result. These sizes are formative, not psychometric validation.
2. Audit incremental valueCompare the frozen current engine with variants that make experience/context/custom facets optional. Keep official score calculation unchanged.Which questions change a useful recommendation, explanation or action? Check false exclusions and distinct task domains; save removed detail as optional where useful.
3. Independent recommendation reviewFreeze model/version and realistic cases before review. Use independent counselors and students; blind reviewers to the intended “correct” answer. Include writing, food, arts/science mixes, dentistry/medicine, no-fit and conflicting preferences.Rubric for relevance, breadth, contradictions, inappropriate exclusions and practical next steps; adjudicated disagreements and held-out cases. Do not tune thresholds simply until a preferred career wins.
4. Official form comparisonIf shortening remains necessary, compare the official 30- and 60-item forms using an appropriate counterbalanced design, permission and expert advice. Avoid letting remembered overlapping items masquerade as independent agreement.Six-score/rank agreement, score uncertainty, changes near thresholds, student understanding and completion. A psychometrician should plan samples/power; do not declare equivalence from a small pilot.
5. Calibration and fairnessRetest after 2–4 weeks, distinguish new exposure from instability; examine profile shape, answer changes and recommendation changes by grade/language/background and familiarity. Use consented, minimized data.No aptitude exclusion from confidence alone; sensible uncertain/mixed results; no unexamined demographic shortcut. Preliminary subgroup samples cannot establish fairness.
6. Finance calibrationRecompute representative employee, professional-training, apprentice, part-time and self-employed cases independently. Reconcile household/year/geography and program costs. Review wage/source changes and school-year tuition updates.Source-dated records, scenario labels, correct tax/debt/aid arithmetic, actual employer schedules where available, and conclusions robust to plausible cost/hour changes.
7. Real usefulness after resultsInvite students to try one activity and revisit in 4–6 weeks; preserve the earlier plan and track what changed.Better understanding, relevant action, ability to compare routes and revise the plan. Choosing our first career suggestion is not itself a success measure. Check that students can still name viable alternatives; include noncompleters in reporting.

A same-task competitor study would add evidence about ease: with authorized access, ask students to find two plausible careers, explain a recommendation, identify training/cost, understand a salary, and save a next action. Compare task success, comprehension and time, not attractiveness alone. This public-document review cannot substitute for that study.

Proposed order of product work

  1. Preserve the friendly flow and measure it. No new required survey sections; keep phone layouts, stacked answers, Back, saving and short transitions.
  2. Shorten custom requirements based on observed value. Keep lifestyle first and the official instrument intact initially; make deeper refinement optional after useful results.
  3. Calibrate recommendations and money claims. Independent review, realistic student pilot, sensitivity checks, and unmistakable pay-scenario definitions.
  4. Strengthen the major/program bridge. Add a few concrete education routes per supported career, real program costs and aid links. Expand missing common careers using demand and breadth, not catalog-size competition.
  5. Add optional learning through action. Short task previews, conversations, clubs/courses, and reflections that update an existing plan.

The most defensible positioning is a clear, evidence-informed guide that helps a teenager understand options and take the next step. We can become more accurate and useful without making the student experience longer or more complicated.
